title: WHY DID MATTHEW MENTION TAMAR, RAHAB, RUTH, AND URIAH’S WIFE BEFORE NAMING MARY?
paragraphs: WHY DID MATTHEW MENTION TAMAR, RAHAB, RUTH, AND URIAH’S WIFE BEFORE NAMING MARY?

Before Matthew gave us the virgin mother and the manger, he opened four doors most families would have preferred to keep locked. And once you understand why, you may never read the genealogy of Jesus the same way again.
Name after name. Generation after generation.
We read it like the credits at the end of a movie.
But Matthew will not let us get to Bethlehem that quickly.
Before he takes us to Mary, he makes us walk through Tamar.
Then a woman he deliberately does not even call by her own name.
Because Matthew is not careless with words.

This is the opening chapter of the New Testament. If you were preparing the royal genealogy of the Messiah—the Son of David, the Son of Abraham—you might expect every embarrassing detail to be polished away.
Instead, Matthew seems to turn the lights on.
He doesn't sanitize the family tree.
Why place these women immediately in the ancestral story that leads to Christ?
Why remind readers of sexual scandal, exploitation, widowhood, prostitution, foreigners, broken promises, royal abuse of power, death, grief, and circumstances that could provoke public suspicion?
And why do all of that before introducing a young woman whose pregnancy would itself appear scandalous to people who did not yet know what God had done?
Maybe because Matthew wants you to understand something before you ever reach the manger:
Jesus did not enter a sanitized human story.
“The book” or “record of the genealogy of Jesus Christ.”
And suddenly Matthew does something striking.
“Ἰούδας δὲ ἐγέννησεν τὸν Φαρὲς καὶ τὸν Ζαρὰ ἐκ τῆς Θαμάρ...”
ἐκ τῆς Θαμάρ — ek tēs Thamar — “by/from Tamar.”
To understand why that name carries weight, you have to go back to Genesis 38.

Tamar had been married to Judah's son Er. Er died. According to the family obligations described in the narrative, Onan was then expected to provide offspring through Tamar for his deceased brother, but he refused to fulfill that obligation faithfully. Onan also died.
Judah then told Tamar to remain a widow until his younger son Shelah grew up.
But Judah did not keep his word.
She eventually disguised herself, and Judah—without recognizing her—slept with her.
When Tamar later became pregnant, Judah was ready to condemn her.
And Judah said words that still cut through centuries of hypocrisy:
The story Matthew invokes is not simply “the scandalous woman Tamar.”
The man carrying the covenant family line.
The man initially prepared to condemn publicly what he had participated in privately.
We can become very good at noticing another person's visible failure while protecting our invisible one.
We can condemn someone else's pregnancy and conceal our own compromise.
We can point toward somebody else's wreckage while quietly hiding the fingerprints we left at the scene.
And through Perez, the genealogy continues.
Then Matthew takes us to another woman.
“Σαλμὼν δὲ ἐγέννησεν τὸν Βόες ἐκ τῆς Ῥαχάβ...”
The woman Joshua identifies as a prostitute in Jericho.
If human beings were editing the Messiah's résumé, this might be where someone whispered:
“Do we really need to mention that?”
Because Rahab's past is not the end of Rahab's story.
And listen to what this Canaanite woman confessed:
“The LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath.”
Her story becomes a story of faith.
So much so that Hebrews 11—the famous chapter celebrating faith—remembers her.
“By faith the prostitute Rahab did not perish...”
James remembers her too when discussing a living faith demonstrated through action.
The woman whose occupation could have become the only label people remembered...
became remembered by Scripture for faith.
Read that again if you have ever believed your worst chapter permanently renamed you.
People may introduce you by what you did.
Jesus knows what His grace can make of you.
People may freeze you in your yesterday.
God is not imprisoned by your yesterday.
And Matthew does not pretend the first did not exist in order to celebrate the second.
Grace is not God pretending sin never mattered.
Grace is God doing what sinners could never do for themselves.
Grace does not call darkness light.
Grace brings sinners out of darkness.
Rahab's story was not powerful because prostitution was harmless.
It was powerful because the mercy of God was greater than the identity her past could have imposed upon her.
“Βόες δὲ ἐγέννησεν τὸν Ἰωβὴδ ἐκ τῆς Ῥούθ...”
An outsider who attached herself to Naomi and to Naomi's God with one of Scripture's most moving declarations:
“Your people shall be my people, and your God my God.”
Ruth arrived in Bethlehem carrying grief.
There was no romantic soundtrack playing behind them.
There were two widows trying to survive.
Ruth went into the fields to glean leftover grain.
He had heard what she had done for Naomi.
And through the beautiful providence unfolded in the book of Ruth, Boaz became her kinsman-redeemer, they married, and Ruth bore Obed.
Obed became the father of Jesse.
The foreign widow gathering leftovers at the edge of somebody else's field becomes the great-grandmother of Israel's greatest king.
You might feel like you are living on the edge of somebody else's field right now.
Wondering how your life could possibly still matter after what you lost.
You cannot see the entire providence of God from the field where you are currently weeping.
But Matthew is still not finished.
Because next comes the most haunting description of all.
ἐκ τῆς τοῦ Οὐρίου — “by/from the [woman] of Uriah.”
Matthew could have written Bathsheba's name.
At minimum, the wording forces the reader to remember Uriah.
And remembering Uriah means remembering 2 Samuel 11.
David attempted to conceal what had happened.
When Uriah refused to cooperate unknowingly with David's cover-up, David arranged for him to be placed where the fighting was fiercest and then abandoned.
Uriah died carrying the consequences of a king's treachery.
David then took Bathsheba as his wife.
But Scripture refuses to let royal power rename evil.
“The thing that David had done displeased the LORD.”
And when Nathan exposed David's sin, he did not flatter the king.
So centuries later, when Matthew writes the genealogy of the Messiah, he does not merely say:
He leaves a verbal scar in the genealogy:
The abuse of royal power mattered.
Repentance does not require pretending the wound never existed.
Forgiveness does not transform evil into good.
Grace does not rewrite history by calling sin righteousness.
Grace rewrites what sin believed would be the final chapter.
Psalm 51 preserves the cry of a broken and repentant man:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
Matthew has one more woman to name.
After generations of fathers fathering sons, Matthew arrives at Joseph.
You expect the same grammatical pattern.
“Ἰακὼβ δὲ ἐγέννησεν τὸν Ἰωσὴφ τὸν ἄνδρα Μαρίας, ἐξ ἧς ἐγεννήθη Ἰησοῦς...”
Jacob fathered Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ.
The relative pronoun is feminine singular.
He does not say Joseph fathered Jesus.
After verse after verse of “A fathered B,” Joseph is identified as Mary's husband, and Jesus is said to have been born from her.
Mary was found to be pregnant “ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου” — ek pneumatos hagiou — “from the Holy Spirit.”
Joseph knew the child was not biologically his.
Before the angel explained what had happened, he intended to divorce Mary quietly rather than expose her publicly.
Imagine Mary standing inside that moment.
She knows what God has done.
But how do you explain a miracle to people who can only see circumstances?
How do you tell your fiancé that your pregnancy is an act of God?
How do you survive the looks?
Matthew has prepared his reader for this moment.
Before Mary, he reminded you about Tamar.
Before Mary, the wife of Uriah.
Women whose stories carried circumstances that could provoke stigma, suspicion, grief, controversy, or social vulnerability.
But here the Gospel announces something utterly unique.
Mary's pregnancy is not the result of sexual immorality.
Matthew explicitly attributes the conception to the Holy Spirit.
“That which is conceived in her is of the Holy Spirit.”
And suddenly the genealogy becomes more than a genealogy.
God has entered the human story.
Not because humanity finally cleaned itself up.
Not because Israel produced a flawless family tree.
Not because David's descendants managed to erase every scandal.
But because God keeps His promises.
Jesus is called the Son of David.
And His very name announces His mission.
The angel tells Joseph to call Him Jesus because “he shall save his people from their sins.”
That is why this cannot become a shallow message saying, “God doesn't care how you live.”
The cross proves sin is more serious than we want to believe.
And the cross proves God's mercy is more astonishing than we dared hope.
Jesus did not come to make peace with our sin.
He came to save us from it.
Rahab's story shows faith reaching beyond a condemned past.
Ruth's story reveals God's providence working through an outsider's grief and faithfulness.
The phrase “wife of Uriah” refuses to let David's power erase the man he wronged.
Mary's story announces the miraculous conception of the Messiah.
We should not flatten their stories into one category.
And Mary was not sexually immoral.
But Matthew deliberately brings these women into the genealogy that leads us to Christ.
And perhaps that is where this genealogy stops being ancient history and begins reading you.
Because somewhere inside these stories is the human ache we keep trying to hide.
Maybe you know what it feels like to be Tamar—failed by someone who should have acted righteously toward you.
Maybe you understand Rahab—the fear that your past will always speak louder than your faith.
Maybe you understand Ruth—trying to remain faithful while carrying grief into an uncertain future.
Maybe you understand what it means to be wounded by someone else's power, choices, or betrayal.
Maybe you understand Mary—obeying God while knowing people may completely misunderstand you.
And that is the one we would rather not admit.
Perhaps you were not merely wounded.
Perhaps there is something hidden behind your Christian vocabulary.
Something deleted from your phone but not from your conscience.
Something you confessed vaguely because naming it honestly terrified you.
Something you keep blaming on stress, loneliness, temptation, your spouse, your childhood, your circumstances...
The Gospel is not only good news for people who have been scandalized.
It is good news for sinners who finally stop hiding.
Sometimes grace begins with the sentence we least want to hear.
You are the one who needs to repent.
All of us stand in need of mercy.
And this is where the genealogy becomes breathtaking.
Jesus' family line contains stories of failure, outsiders, grief, brokenness, royal sin, judgment, repentance, providence, and mercy...
yet Jesus Himself does not arrive as another sinner needing redemption.
He enters the story without becoming corrupted by its sin.
The genealogy leads to the One who will carry a cross.
The Son of David will wear a crown of thorns.
The promised King will be mocked as a criminal.
The sinless One will give His life for sinners.
The One whose genealogy contains stories people might want hidden will eventually hang publicly exposed before the world.
And there, at Calvary, God does not sweep sin underneath history's carpet.
This is why your scandal does not have to become your final identity.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by helping us pretend nothing happened.
He changes where we are going.
Christian grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
It is the miracle that, through Christ, sinners can be changed.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe you thought this article was about four women in an ancient genealogy.
you found your own secret sitting between the names.
The pornography you keep returning to.
The bitterness you have learned to call discernment.
The resentment hidden behind your smile.
The church wound you never processed.
The secret fear that if people knew the complete story, they would never look at you the same way again.
Jesus already knows the complete story.
And still the Gospel invitation stands.
Clean yourself up enough to deserve Him.
Bring Him the sin you have excused and the wounds you cannot repair yourself.
There is forgiveness in Jesus Christ.
There is cleansing in Jesus Christ.
There is reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
There is no past so impressive that it can save you.
And there is no repentant sinner whose sin is stronger than the saving sufficiency of Christ.

So maybe Matthew placed those names where he did because before we meet the virgin mother, before Bethlehem, before the wise men, before the Sermon on the Mount, before the miracles, before Gethsemane, before Golgotha...
we need to know what kind of world Jesus came into.
And into this world came Jesus Christ.
That is the scandal of grace.
But that sin did not stop God from fulfilling His promise.
Not that everybody in the genealogy was innocent.
Not that everybody's circumstances were the same.
But that the sovereign purposes of God moved through generations of profoundly human history until, in the fullness of God's plan, Christ came.
So stop believing that Jesus is waiting for a more presentable version of you before you can come to Him.
The Gospel has never been about convincing God that you are good enough.
It is the announcement that the Savior has come.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, don't manufacture a dramatic response for people to see. Give God the honest one.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to discover that Christians are not people without scars.
We are people who know where mercy is found.

And if someone came to mind while you were reading—someone drowning in shame, someone convinced their past disqualifies them, someone far from God, someone wounded by church, someone who believes Jesus could never want them—send this to them.
There may come a night when the old accusation returns and tells you that your worst chapter gets the final word.
It is not a replacement for obedience to Christ.
It is not a purchase of God's favor.
It does not buy blessing, salvation, forgiveness, answered prayer, or spiritual status.
Your giving belongs ultimately under your obedience to God, guided by Scripture, wisdom, generosity, and a willing heart.

Scripture celebrates willing generosity and material partnership in Gospel ministry. Paul thanked believers who partnered with him in the work of the Gospel, while Christian giving is to be willing rather than coerced—“not reluctantly or under compulsion.”
We do not want your support because someone frightened or pressured you into giving.
If you cannot financially support the ministry, please do not believe that makes your part meaningless.
Send it personally to someone who needs Christ.
Tell somebody what Jesus has done for you.
Because the goal was never to build an audience around Gospel Warrior.
The goal is to point an audience toward Jesus Christ.
So when the enemy points at the chapter you wish could disappear, remember this:

Jesus does not need an edited genealogy to be the Savior—and He does not need an edited version of your story before you come to Him. Bring Him the truth, because grace does its most beautiful work where hiding finally ends.
